rv.q: Ian Rickson, a byword for directorial meticulousness, has taken the plunge with a West End production of revelatory finesse.
Ian Rickson’s production is expertly paced, and there are vivid supporting performances.
And she’s pretty much pulled it off.
However, for all the turbulent emotions on display, Ian Rickson’s production feels frustratingly stiff and static.
Emotionally, it flays the flesh off the play, in large part thanks to Atwell's excoriating performance.
This is still a deft revival, mining a classic work for gripping modern drama.
Ibsen's sometimes-murky psychology here rivets throughout, even without the numerous "play for today" cues that get signalled along the way.
The detail of the playing and the flair of the staging – the ending is as brilliant as it is shocking – make a strong case for this play and its heady mix of sex and politics.

The curtain rises to reveal a stunningly detailed and evocative set, the interior of a hauntingly shadowed and seemingly twilit, dust sheet covered room. The walls were hung with many partially obscured portraits, the wooden floors looked ancient and worn to smoothness.
Hayley Atwell shines as Rebecca, fully embodying her struggle between idealistic beliefs and love for Rosmer.

In Ibsen's world, and even more so in Macmillan's, politics is in thrall to the power of the celebrity endorsement, as both Kroll and his rival Mortensgaard (Jake Fairbrother) whirl between desiring Rosmer's backing, and seeking to bring him down if he does not give it.
Rosmersholm is really enjoyable. It's visually epic and shamelessly so.
The air in Ian Rickson's atmospheric production is thick with the stultifying social values embodied by Rosmer's judgmental brother-in-law Kroll.

cn.t: Critics praise this timely West End revival of Ibsen's rarely staged play, lauding Macmillan's sharp adaptation and stellar performances from Atwell and Burke that make the 1886 work feel urgently relevant to today's political turbulence.
